passage: Biochemists in the Hartwell laboratory characterized hexokinase purified from a bacterial expression system, focusing on its response to a candidate small-molecule inhibitor designed to resemble glucose. Reactions contained a fixed enzyme concentration in buffered solution at 25 °C, and initial velocities were measured at six glucose concentrations with and without 120 µM inhibitor. Product formation was followed spectrophotometrically for the first 60 seconds, a window in which less than 5% of substrate was consumed. Each velocity represents the mean of three independent reactions, and the standard error was below 4% of every mean. The team wished to determine whether the compound binds the free enzyme at the active site or instead binds elsewhere, and to estimate its dissociation constant for the enzyme–inhibitor complex before testing it in cultured cells. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and the buffer contained no metal chelators or reducing agents that could interfere with the assay. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

questions.stem: According to Table 1, what is the initial velocity in the presence of inhibitor when [S] = 100 µM?
questions.explanation: Reading the inhibitor column at [S] = 100 µM gives 30 µmol/min; the control column value (40) is the uninhibited rate.
questions.trap: Reading the no-inhibitor column (40 µmol/min) instead of the inhibitor column, which gives 30 µmol/min at 100 µM.

questions.stem: Which additional experiment would best distinguish competitive from noncompetitive inhibition by this compound?

options.A: Measure product formation after 60 minutes rather than 60 seconds
options.B: Repeat the assay at a lower temperature to see whether inhibition disappears
options.C: Measure velocity at a single substrate concentration with several enzyme concentrations
options.D: Measure whether very high substrate concentrations restore the uninhibited maximal velocity

questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, so sufficiently high [S] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax regardless of [S].
questions.trap: Choosing a 60-minute measurement; a longer run changes substrate depletion but does not show whether high [S] restores Vmax.

questions.stem: Assuming simple competitive inhibition, what is the approximate Ki of the inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). Here Km,app/Km = 2, so [I]/Ki = 1 and Ki = 120/1 = 120 µM.
questions.trap: Multiplying [I] by the 2-fold Km shift (120 × 2 = 240 µM) instead of solving 2 = 1 + [I]/Ki, which gives Ki = 120 µM.

questions.stem: Which statement about the data is NOT consistent with competitive inhibition?

options.A: The inhibitor binds the free enzyme in preference to the enzyme–substrate complex
options.B: The apparent Km is larger in the presence of the inhibitor
options.C: The inhibition is weaker at higher substrate concentrations
options.D: The maximal velocity extrapolated to infinite [S] is lower with the inhibitor

questions.explanation: Correct: D. In competitive inhibition Vmax is unchanged (60 µmol/min in both data sets); only the apparent Km rises (50 to 100 µM). Why the others are wrong: A) a competitive inhibitor binds free enzyme, not the enzyme–substrate complex. B) the apparent Km doubles. C) velocities converge as [S] rises (6.7/12 at 12.5 versus 48/53.3 at 400).
questions.trap: Expecting inhibition to be equally strong at all [S]; for a competitive inhibitor, substrate overcomes it and velocities converge at high [S].

questions.stem: Many drugs, such as statins and methotrexate, act as competitive inhibitors. Which property of such drugs most directly explains why they are often structural analogs of the substrate?

options.A: They must occupy the same active site as the substrate
options.B: They must bind the enzyme–substrate complex only
options.C: They must lower the enzyme's turnover number at saturating substrate
options.D: They must bind covalently to the enzyme

questions.explanation: Competition requires binding to the same site; structural similarity to the substrate (or transition state) lets the drug fit the active site and compete reversibly.
questions.trap: Assuming drugs must bind covalently; reversible competitive inhibitors bind the same active site noncovalently.
